## 1 Business understanding and study scope

This course project compares methods for classifying the recorded status of eye
cancer cases as Active, In Remission, or Deceased. The business question is whether
baseline characteristics in this teaching dataset contain enough signal to
classify those statuses better than a simple baseline. The practical output is a
comparison of algorithms and ensembles, with reproducible evaluation and explicit
limitations. There is no clinical deployment in this project.

The dataset was obtained from the Kaggle Eye Cancer Patient Records listing:
<https://www.kaggle.com/datasets/ak0212/eye-cancer-patient-records>.
The original course analysis describes the data as simulated. I therefore treat
it as a simulated teaching dataset; provenance and license terms should be
confirmed at the source before reuse outside this exercise. It is not an
independently validated clinical cohort. Dataset approval was a course requirement;
this repository does not independently establish that approval was received.

I exclude survival duration and treatment variables. Their availability at a
prediction time is not established, so retaining them would make a prospective
interpretation difficult to defend. Even the retained features do not establish
a valid clinical prediction timeline. This remains a retrospective teaching
exercise, not a prognosis tool.

## 2 Data understanding and quality assessment

```{r load-data}
raw <- read_project_data(root)
x <- make_predictors(raw)
y <- raw$Outcome_Status
quality <- data.frame(
  Field = names(raw),
  Missing = vapply(raw, function(v) sum(is.na(v)), integer(1)),
  Unique = vapply(raw, function(v) length(unique(v)), integer(1))
)
knitr::kable(quality)
```

There are `r nrow(raw)` records. IDs must be unique, outcome labels must be present
and recognized, and nonmissing ages must be positive and finite. The pipeline
stops on violations instead of silently deleting cases. Missing numeric
predictors are median-imputed using training rows. Missing categorical values
receive a separate category. The literal marker value “None” is retained as a
recorded category; interpreting it as an absent test, an absent mutation, or a
missing result would require a data dictionary. I do not assume these meanings
are interchangeable. No outlier clipping is applied without a defensible domain
threshold.

## 3 Split strategy and training-only exploration

All algorithms use the same stratified 70/30 outer split. The split and fold
assignments are saved with patient IDs. Five stratified folds within the training
partition are used for tuning; a smoke run uses three folds on a small subset.
The test partition is reserved for final comparisons. Preprocessing is refitted
inside each fold and each bootstrap sample.

```{r split-and-explore}
train_idx <- stratified_split(y)
train_x <- x[train_idx, , drop = FALSE]
train_y <- y[train_idx]
folds <- make_folds(train_y, k = 5L)
knitr::kable(as.data.frame(table(train_y)), col.names = c("Training outcome", "Count"))
summary(train_x$Age)
```

```{r training-eda, fig.width=7, fig.height=4}
barplot(table(train_y), ylab = "Training records", col = "steelblue",
        main = "Training outcome distribution")
boxplot(train_x$Age ~ train_y, xlab = "Recorded outcome", ylab = "Age",
        main = "Age by recorded outcome in training data", col = "lightgray")
```

These plots describe this training sample. They do not establish causal effects,
clinical representativeness, or predictive usefulness. Model comparisons below
provide the relevant predictive evidence.

## 4 Model-specific data shaping

The predictors include age, an age-group transformation with fixed cutoffs,
gender, cancer type, laterality, stage, genetic-marker category, family history,
and country. IDs, diagnosis dates, survival duration, and treatment variables
are excluded. Country and other demographic fields can reflect sampling or
social context; this exercise does not establish fairness across subgroups.

| Algorithm | Input representation | Reason |
|---|---|---|
| Regularized multinomial logistic regression | One-hot categories and standardized numeric matrix | Numeric design matrix; scaling makes the decay penalty more comparable across columns |
| kNN | The same standardized encoded matrix | Euclidean distances require numeric inputs and comparable scales |
| Random forest | Imputed numeric columns and categorical factors | Native factor handling avoids imposing an arbitrary integer order |
| XGBoost | One-hot numeric matrix without scaling | Numeric inputs are required; tree splits do not need standardization |

I use `nnet::multinom` with tuned decay for the logistic model. This replaces the
previous mix of glmnet for one fit and an unpenalized multinomial fit for bagging,
so the base learner and its bagged version now use the same modeling procedure.
I remove the earlier PCA transformation: it was fitted before splitting, and PCA
is not required for this modest feature set. Zero-variance encoded columns are
removed based on fit rows only. kNN retains the encoded categorical predictors
rather than accidentally dropping them.

```{r shaping-example}
prep <- fit_preprocessor(train_x)
lr_matrix <- transform_predictors(prep, train_x, "lr")
rf_frame <- transform_predictors(prep, train_x, "rf")
xgb_matrix <- transform_predictors(prep, train_x, "xgb")
data.frame(Representation = c("Scaled encoded", "Native factors", "Unscaled encoded"),
           Rows = c(nrow(lr_matrix), nrow(rf_frame), nrow(xgb_matrix)),
           Columns = c(ncol(lr_matrix), ncol(rf_frame), ncol(xgb_matrix)))
```

The example above fits on the outer training data for illustration. Tuning does
**not** reuse that preprocessor: every fold learns its own imputation, category
mapping, zero-variance filter, and scaling using only that fold's training rows.
Previously unseen categorical values map to a novel category. Dummy columns
constant in fit rows are removed; unseen categories consequently contribute no
learned category-specific coefficient.

## 5 Model fitting and hyperparameter tuning

Random forests use a fixed minimum terminal-node size of 10 and a maximum of
64 terminal nodes per tree to limit tree complexity and keep repeated bootstrap
runs practical. These limits are fixed before held-out evaluation.

The four algorithms cover linear decision boundaries, local similarity, bagged
trees, and boosted trees. XGBoost supplies the boosting component. Each tuning
candidate is compared using mean macro-F1 across the same training folds. A
single fixed seed schedule makes comparisons reproducible. Grid ties select the
first listed candidate; test performance does not choose hyperparameters.

```{r tuning-grids}
model_grids(smoke = params$smoke)
```

```{r tuning-implementation, code=deparse(tune_model), eval=FALSE}
```

```{r learner-implementation, code=deparse(fit_engine), eval=FALSE}
```

## 6 Homogeneous and heterogeneous ensembles

For each algorithm, I fit stratified bootstrap replicas with replacement and
average their class probabilities. This is a homogeneous ensemble because every
replica uses the same algorithm. The full run uses 30 replicas per algorithm;
the smoke test uses two. Random forest already uses bootstrap trees internally;
outer bagging of forests is included to make the assignment's per-algorithm
bagging requirement explicit. Bagging XGBoost also is additional to boosting,
not a replacement for it. These extra fits are not presumed to improve results.

```{r bagging-implementation, code=deparse(bag_probabilities), eval=FALSE}
```

The heterogeneous soft-voting ensemble averages probabilities from the four
bagged learners with equal weights fixed in advance. It combines different
algorithms as required. I also evaluate a separate stacked ensemble built from
the four unbagged learners. Its meta-model is trained on out-of-fold predictions
from training patients only. Each such prediction comes from a base fit that
excluded that patient's fold. The final base fits then predict the held-out test
patients, and the meta-model combines those predictions. The test labels are
never used to train the stack.

The following excerpt shows the training/evaluation boundary inside the runner;
`oof` contains training-only predictions, and `base_probs` contains held-out
predictions. The complete implementation is in `src/ml_pipeline.R`.

```{r stack-implementation, eval=FALSE}
meta_train <- data.frame(Outcome_Status = train_y, meta_features(oof))
meta_model <- nnet::multinom(Outcome_Status ~ ., data = meta_train,
                            decay = 1, maxit = 1000, trace = FALSE)
stack_probs <- predict(meta_model, newdata = meta_features(base_probs), type = "probs")
vote_probs <- Reduce("+", bagged_probs) / length(bagged_probs)
```

OOF predictions use hyperparameters chosen within the outer training partition.
Their training scores are not claimed as unbiased estimates after that selection.
The outer held-out test provides the final comparison. The stack's decay is fixed
at 1 rather than chosen by checking test performance.

## 7 Run the experiment and evaluate

```{r run-analysis}
if (params$rerun) {
  result <- run_experiment(raw, outdir, smoke = params$smoke)
} else {
  status <- file.path(outdir, "run_status.txt")
  if (!file.exists(status) || !identical(readLines(status), "COMPLETE"))
    stop("No complete run found; render with rerun = TRUE.")
  config <- dget(file.path(outdir, "run_config.R"))
  if (!identical(config$data_md5,
                 unname(tools::md5sum(file.path(root, "data", "eye_cancer_patients.csv")))) ||
      !identical(config$code_md5, unname(tools::md5sum(file.path(root, "src", "ml_pipeline.R")))))
    stop("Data or analysis code changed; rerun the experiment.")
  result <- readRDS(file.path(outdir, "analysis.rds"))
  result$comparison <- result$metrics
}
knitr::kable(result$comparison, digits = 3)
```

**Run mode: `r mode`.** `r if (params$smoke) "These are small-subset smoke-test results, not final model performance." else "These are results from the full dataset with the fixed held-out split."`

Macro-F1 gives every class equal weight. Accuracy, macro precision, macro recall,
per-class results, and confusion matrices provide complementary views. A class
with no predicted positives receives precision and F1 of zero rather than being
silently omitted. The majority baseline is chosen from training counts. A second baseline samples
labels using training class proportions with a fixed seed; it represents a
classifier with no patient-specific signal. Baseline
macro-F1 need not equal 1/3; the pipeline computes it from actual predictions.

```{r metric-implementation, code=deparse(score_predictions), eval=FALSE}
```

```{r compare-plot, fig.width=9, fig.height=5}
comparison <- result$comparison
par(mar = c(5, 14, 3, 1))
barplot(comparison$Macro_F1, names.arg = comparison$Model, horiz = TRUE,
        las = 1, xlim = c(0, 1), xlab = "Held-out macro-F1", col = "steelblue",
        main = paste("Model comparison", mode, "run"))
```

```{r per-class-results}
knitr::kable(result$per_class, digits = 3, row.names = FALSE)
```

```{r confusion-matrices}
confusions <- if (!is.null(result$confusion)) result$confusion else lapply(result$scored, `[[`, "confusion")
confusions
```

## 8 Interpretation and limitations

```{r interpret-results, results='asis'}
best <- comparison[which.max(comparison$Macro_F1), ]
baseline <- comparison$Macro_F1[comparison$Model == "Majority baseline"]
cat(sprintf("The largest observed macro-F1 in this %s run is **%.3f** for **%s**. Its difference from the majority baseline is **%+.3f**.\n\n",
            mode, best$Macro_F1, best$Model, best$Macro_F1 - baseline))
random_baseline <- comparison$Macro_F1[comparison$Model == "Stratified random baseline"]
cat(sprintf("The stratified random baseline scored %.3f; the best observed score differs from it by %+.3f.\n\n", random_baseline, best$Macro_F1 - random_baseline))
cat("This is a descriptive comparison on one fixed split. It does not establish statistical superiority, clinical usefulness, or generalization to other patients. Selecting the largest test score is not permission to retune on that test set.\n\n")
for (kind in names(result$tuning)) {
  z <- result$tuning[[kind]]
  selected <- z$table[z$best_row, , drop = FALSE]
  cat(sprintf("For **%s**, the selected training-CV mean macro-F1 was %.3f. The grid and its fold-to-fold SD are saved in `tuning_%s.csv`.\n\n",
              kind, selected$CV_Macro_F1, kind))
}
```

The simulated data and uncertain timing of outcome assessment limit interpretation.
A modest score is a useful result when reported honestly; it does not by itself
prove that the implementation is correct or that the features lack signal.
The regression tests, saved predictions, and reproducible commands are separate
checks on correctness. No claim is made that stacking or bagging must improve
over individual models. There is no external validation, calibrated clinical risk
estimate, subgroup fairness assessment, or evidence of deployment readiness.
Future work would require a clearly timed prediction target and an appropriate
independent cohort, not simply a larger ensemble.

## 9 Reproducibility and assignment coverage

The complete implementation is in `src/ml_pipeline.R`; the notebook displays the
main fitting, tuning, bagging, and scoring code alongside the explanations. The
command-line entry point executes the same implementation. CSV files record
split assignments, tuning grids, predictions, class probabilities, and metrics.
`run_status.txt` must say COMPLETE before outputs are interpreted as a finished
run. `sessionInfo.txt` records actual package versions and `run_config.R` records
seeds, settings, data and code fingerprints. Fitted models are not deployed.

| Assignment component | Evidence |
|---|---|
| Dataset approval | Must be confirmed from course records; not inferred here |
| At least three algorithms and separate shaping | Four learners and explicit representations |
| Boosting and tuning | XGBoost plus training-only CV grids |
| Bagging and homogeneous ensembles | Bootstrap ensembles for all four learners |
| CRISP-DM and journal | Question, data audit, preparation, modeling, evaluation, limitations |
| Heterogeneous ensemble | Equal-weight soft voting and OOF stacking |
| Metrics and interpretation | Common held-out split, baseline, class metrics and dynamic report |
